segment_name: Opening: The Boy Who Would Become a Man

questions.question: Oliver, let's start with you because you've said something that I think is going to set the cat among the pigeons — you've called this novel 'genius-level entertainment' and you want us to hear it rather than just read it. Can you take us into that passage in chapter six — the 'kind word' passage — and actually perform it for us? What does it sound like when Dickens is doing something this emotionally sophisticated?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c6:p28 aloud and demonstrate his thesis about rhythm and performance, setting up the contrast with Edmund's moral-philosophical reading and Daniel's structural reading

questions.question: Edmund, I could hear you bristling slightly just now. Because Oliver just called that passage 'theater' — David performing regret. But my understanding is you think that undersells what's actually happening there. Is Dickens doing psychology or performance? And does it matter?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's counter-thesis that this is genuine moral insight not theatrical effect, provoke the Leigh vs Trevelyan disagreement about whether form or content is primary

questions.question: Daniel, I want to bring you in here because you've said something quite provocative in our chat — that when David looks back and says one kind word could have remade him entirely, you think that's actually Dickens showing us a character who *still doesn't understand what happened to him*. That's a pretty dark reading. Are you saying David Copperfield is a novel about a man who never quite wakes up?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to articulate his false consciousness argument and his claim that Murdstone's cruelty is rational and structural, provoking strong reactions from both Edmund and Oliver who both locate redemption or growth in the novel

questions.question: Let's talk about Miss Mowcher, because she arrives in this strange, grotesque physical comedy — her finger can't reach her nose, she waddles, she's almost impossible to picture — and yet Edmund, you've said that passage is actually the novel's moral education in miniature. What's Dickens actually asking us to do when he describes her like that?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to read or paraphrase the Mowcher introduction from c24:p83 and articulate his thesis about moral imagination vs appearance, then let Daniel push back on the 'visual grammar of dispossession' reading

questions.question: Right, and Daniel I know you want to go somewhere quite different with Betsey's financial disasters — the pigs to a foreign market, the diving way, the mining way. Edmund thinks it's a portrait of a woman who knows herself without self-pity. Oliver thinks the comedy is load-bearing plot machinery. You've said it's actually about dispossession. Can those three readings all be true at once, or does one of them kill the others?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or productive collision on the Betsey passage, ending the segment with all three positions in active tension rather than resolved

steering_notes: The big fault line in this segment is between Edmund's moral-individualist reading, Oliver's performative-entertainment reading, and Daniel's structural-power reading — and all three converge on the same two or three passages. The host's job is to keep routing back to the actual text whenever the conversation goes too abstract. If Edmund and Daniel are arguing about whether kindness matters structurally, get Oliver to read a clause aloud — that resets the energy. Watch for Daniel steamrolling: his arguments are the most systematically developed and he can crowd out the others. Give Edmund room to be indignant; he's at his best when slightly annoyed. The Mowcher question is the wildcard — all three have genuinely different readings and none of them are obviously wrong, so let that one breathe.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Murdstone 'simply chooses cruelty' directly contradicts Daniel's argument that cruelty is structurally rational — this should produce the segment's best argument if the host can get them to speak directly to each other rather than past each other

Oliver's insistence that c6:p28 is 'performance of regret' rather than psychological realism is a direct provocation to Edmund, who reads it as the deepest moral insight in the book — worth naming explicitly

Daniel's reading of Betsey's losses as structural dispossession and Edmund's reading of them as lucid self-knowledge are not just different but mutually exclusive — one of them has to be wrong, or Dickens has to be doing two things at once

Oliver's point that comedy sets up 'real jeopardy' in the Betsey passage is a potential bridge between Edmund and Daniel — he might be the one who reconciles them, or he might get caught in the crossfire

questions.question: Daniel, you used a phrase in our pre-chat that stuck with me — you said the placard isn't teaching David empathy, it's teaching him that shame is a *technology of control*. But here's what I keep coming back to: David survives. He becomes a successful novelist. Doesn't that complicate the story you're telling? If the machine is this totalizing, why does it produce a David Copperfield at all?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to commit hard to the infrastructure-of-humiliation thesis, then expose the tension with the novel's bildungsroman arc — this sets up Oliver and Edmund to push back immediately

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read the Miss Murdstone denial scene — that incredible list of negatives, 'not at all alike, exactly unlike, utterly dissimilar' — as comic theatre, written for an actor's voice. But Daniel's sitting there thinking the *vehemence* is the confession, that the fury is what shows us how much work goes into keeping class distinctions intact. Are those two readings actually in conflict, or is that what makes Dickens so slippery?
questions.intent: Force Oliver to defend theatrical performance against structural critique — get him to read the passage aloud and then defend why tone matters as much as content

questions.question: Edmund, you've said the placard scene is fundamentally about conscience — that David's torment is a creature of imagination, not of what anyone actually does to him. But Daniel would say you're letting the system off the hook by psychologizing what is actually a deliberate act of institutional marking. I'm curious: does it *matter* to your reading who put the placard there and why?
questions.intent: Push Edmund to distinguish between psychological and systemic readings of shame — aim to provoke the clearest possible statement of his conscience-and-soul thesis so Daniel can respond

questions.question: Let's talk about Emily's letters, because this is where I think you three are furthest apart. Daniel, you called her letters her *own execution* — she internalizes the moral verdict and performs her own erasure. Edmund thinks they show genuine moral self-knowledge and something close to redemption. Oliver thinks the fragmented sentences are just how desperation actually sounds — that Dickens *respects* her enough to let her be inarticulate. Can you make the case that what reads like repentance is actually something darker?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to read or paraphrase the Emily letter passages and commit to the most unsentimental reading possible — then let Edmund and Oliver respond with their competing readings

questions.question: Oliver, you mentioned the emigrant ship passage as something almost tender — Dickens holding death and life in a single image. But Daniel sees those same people as the *disposable*, the ones society has already written off. And Edmund thinks the passage is almost Scriptural, visionary in a way that has nothing to do with policy or reform. So what is Dickens actually doing when he puts us on that ship — is he mourning, condemning, or transcending?
questions.intent: Use the emigrant ship passage as a lightning rod for all three interpretive frameworks simultaneously — get all three experts debating the same sentences with completely different frameworks

steering_notes: The segment has a natural fault line: Daniel reads social structure, Edmund reads individual conscience, Oliver reads theatrical performance — and all three can be right about the same passage, which is both the segment's richness and its risk. Push toward moments where they have to account for each other's evidence, not just restate their own frame. If it gets too abstract, pull back to specific sentences — ask someone to read a passage aloud. The Miss Murdstone list and the placard paranoia sentence are both good for this. Watch for Edmund and Daniel to talk past each other using the word 'shame' to mean completely different things — that's worth surfacing explicitly. Keep Oliver in the mix; he can play mediator between the other two but has his own strong line that deserves pressure.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver says Dickens *performs* shame for the reader through rhythm and repetition; Daniel says that same performance is panopticon logic before Foucault — they're describing the same textual effect and drawing opposite conclusions about what it means

Edmund argues Emily's letters show genuine moral agency and self-knowledge; Daniel argues they show the system colonizing the victim's own voice — both read the fragmented syntax closely but arrive at redemption vs. erasure

Daniel claims the Doctors' Commons somnolence is the feature not the bug — it works perfectly to exclude the poor; Oliver thinks Dickens has actual affection for the ritual and its dignity — this is a direct conflict worth staging

Edmund says the emigrant ship has nothing to do with policy or reform; Daniel says it's the only passage where the system is honest about what it produces; Oliver says it's tender — three entirely different emotional registers for the same image

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our pre-chat that I keep turning over — that the real seduction in this section isn't Steerforth seducing Em'ly, it's Dickens seducing *us*. Can you take us to that passage you wanted to read — the one where David's looking back on this whole period with such tenderness — and show us exactly what you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c35:p110 and establish the central thesis that Dickens implicates the reader in Steerforth's charm — sets up the whole segment's argument and gives Edmund and Daniel something to respond to

questions.question: Edmund, you agree that David is complicit here, but you put it very differently — you called it a failure of *gratitude*, almost a moral failing in a quite old-fashioned sense. And you want to quote something about Peggotty being 'the best, the most faithful' — David's own words. Doesn't that make it *worse*, not better? He *knows* what she is to him and still lets Steerforth in?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's strongest take on gratitude as the cardinal virtue and David's self-deception — and create tension with Oliver's more aesthetic reading by pushing on whether knowledge-plus-failure is more damning than simple blindness

questions.question: Daniel, you've been very patient but I suspect you want to blow up the whole frame here — because both Oliver and Edmund are essentially talking about David's *psychology*, his charm, his blindness, his guilt. And you're saying: hang on, that's the cover story. What's the passage you want to throw at us — the one about David being ashamed of Peggotty?
questions.intent: Let Daniel introduce the class argument and the shame passage (c15:p132) as a direct challenge to both Oliver's aesthetic reading and Edmund's moral reading — creates maximum three-way tension

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel just said Steerforth isn't the villain — he's the *system being honest*. That Em'ly's ruin and David's happiness aren't in tension, they're actually the same transaction. I think you find that reading genuinely wrong, not just incomplete — so make the case against it.
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Edmund's moral-imagination reading and Daniel's structural reading — Edmund's pre-interview specifically prepared to push back on exactly this point, should produce real heat

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Oliver, you said David's nostalgia in that 'trifles make the sum of life' passage is somehow written *in Steerforth's voice*, in his cadence. Edmund hears it as tragic wisdom. Daniel hears it as David congratulating himself on domestic happiness that Em'ly paid for. Can you read it out loud and then tell me: whose voice is it?
questions.intent: Create a three-way close-reading showdown on c55:p52 — the same passage all three experts want to quote, for completely different reasons — maximum cross-engagement, strong radio ending

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-act structure: start with Oliver's aesthetic seduction argument (we're all complicit as readers), let Edmund complicate it with moral weight, then let Daniel detonate the class argument underneath both of them. The real fireworks will come when Edmund and Daniel go directly at each other — Edmund thinks Daniel's structural reading lets David off the hook morally; Daniel thinks Edmund's moral reading is sentimental and ignores power. Oliver is the useful wild card who can reframe either argument by pulling it back to the text and Dickens's craft. Don't let this become a sociology seminar — keep returning to specific passages and the question of whose *voice* we're hearing in the narration.
cross_engagement_targets: All three experts want to quote c55:p52 ('trifles make the sum of life') but for completely incompatible reasons — Oliver hears Steerforth's cadence, Edmund hears tragic moral wisdom, Daniel hears class-protected sentimentality. Hold this for the final question and let them fight over the same lines.

Edmund's claim that David's shame of Peggotty is a *moral failure* directly contradicts Daniel's claim that it's a *structural inevitability* — push Edmund to say whether the class system exculpates David or not

Oliver's argument that Dickens seduces the reader through charm implicitly agrees with Daniel that the novel is complicit — but Oliver celebrates this as artistic genius while Daniel treats it as ideological failure. Neither has fully reckoned with the other's version of 'complicity'

c23:p118 (Mrs. Gummidge clapping) is flagged by all three experts as pivotal but they read it differently: Oliver sees ironic stage direction, Edmund sees the exact moment corruption enters, Daniel sees intact working-class joy about to be destroyed by a class predator. A direct question about what that clapping *means* could be devastating.

segment_name: Comedy and Cruelty: The Art of Dickens's Wit

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Creakle's whispered voice in c8:p4 is hilarious *because* it's sinister and sinister *because* it's funny — that you can't actually separate the two. Can you read us that passage and show us what you mean? Because I think some people hear 'Dickens is funny' and assume the comedy is sort of decorating something more serious underneath.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage aloud and make his strongest case that comedy and cruelty share the same DNA — sets up the central tension of the segment and baits Daniel into disagreeing

questions.question: Daniel, I can hear you itching to jump in there. Because you've got a very different read on what that whisper is doing — you're saying it's not just grotesque comedy, it's actually the sound of a specific kind of power, a bankrupt hop-dealer who's been handed children's bodies as compensation. Is Oliver's reading letting Dickens off the hook a little?
questions.intent: Force the direct disagreement between Daniel and Oliver — is the comedy humanizing or obscuring? Draw out Daniel's point about c8:p47 as the passage that refuses to let us laugh

questions.question: Edmund, you've called c8:p46 — the dormitory feast, the moonlight, the phosphorus box — a meditation on how fear and secrecy create intimacy, something morally neutral. But Daniel is essentially arguing the opposite: that Dickens is making the boys complicit in glamorizing their own subjection. Who's right? What's actually happening in that scene?
questions.intent: Triangulate the three positions — Edmund's moral-psychological reading versus Daniel's ideological one, with Oliver's aesthetic argument hovering over both. Get Edmund to quote the 'mysterious feeling' passage

questions.question: Edmund, you want to end this whole arc — the school, the dormitory, the cruelty — at David's remorse in c26:p50, that 'horror of having committed a thousand offences I had forgotten.' You're saying that's Dickens's real subject: conscience, not institutions. But Oliver, you've said the same David who gets drunk and disgraces himself is the same David who suffers exquisitely, and that contradiction is the engine of the whole novel. Is the remorse the point, or is it just the hangover?
questions.intent: Push on whether David's moral education is genuinely redemptive or whether Dickens keeps us laughing at David even as he suffers — create a three-way collision on c26:p50

questions.question: Daniel, last one for you — and it's a provocation. Oliver says Dickens is 'the greatest entertainer of guilt in English literature.' You seem to be saying the guilt he entertains is the wrong guilt — we feel bad for David, we laugh at Creakle, and meanwhile the actual machinery of class violence just hums along invisibly. Is Dickens's comedy ultimately on the side of the system it's mocking?
questions.intent: End the segment on the sharpest possible question — forces Daniel to either fully commit to his most radical position or qualify it, and gives Oliver and Edmund the chance to defend Dickens in completely different ways

steering_notes: The segment's engine is a three-way disagreement about what Dickens's comedy is *for* — Oliver says it's the moral point itself, Daniel says it's camouflage for class violence, Edmund says it's the instrument of individual conscience. Let Oliver perform passages aloud wherever possible; his point about Dickens being written for the ear needs to be demonstrated not just argued. Keep nudging Daniel back to c8:p47 as his key text — that's where his reading is strongest and most uncomfortable. Watch for Edmund sentimentalizing the mother-at-the-gate passage; it's beautiful but it risks going soft. The best radio moment will be when Oliver and Daniel have to agree on the same passage meaning opposite things.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver argues comedy humanizes cruelty; Daniel argues it makes cruelty invisible — they want to quote the *same* passage (c8:p4) to opposite ends. Let them fight over a four-word sentence.

Daniel says the dormitory scene (c8:p46) trains boys to find beauty in their own subjection; Edmund says it's morally neutral intimacy born of transgression. This is the sharpest direct contradiction in the pre-interviews and needs a dedicated question.

Edmund reads David's remorse in c26:p50 as the novel's true destination; Oliver insists the drunk-and-offensive David and the suffering David are the same person and you can't resolve the comedy into redemption that cleanly — push them to square off on this directly.
Daniel will likely dismiss Edmund's reading of the mother at the gate (c10:p156) as sentimentality masking structural powerlessness — if Edmund quotes it, invite Daniel to respond immediately.

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that's been rattling around in my head — that David is *lying* when he says 'there is no alloy of self in what I feel for you,' and that the sentence rhythm is actually *performing* that lie. Can you read that line and show us what you mean? Because to most readers, that's the emotional climax. The moment David finally gets it right.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to do a close reading of the 'no alloy of self' line as unreliable narration, establishing the segment's central tension before Edmund and Daniel wade in with their very different readings of the same passage

questions.question: Edmund, I suspect you heard that and wanted to throw something. Because your reading of that same line is almost the opposite — you called it the 'fruit of David's entire moral education,' a moment of genuine achieved selflessness. So who's right? Is David lying to himself, or has he actually got there?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Edmund's moral-transcendence reading and Oliver's unreliable-narrator reading of the same passage — the disagreement here is fundamental and should generate real heat

questions.question: Daniel, I want to bring you in on the schoolroom passage, because you and Edmund are looking at the same room — the litter, the trapped mice, the caged bird — and seeing completely different things. Edmund says those mice are David's own ego, his inner captivity to illusion. You say they're what class discipline actually looks like. Can you read the passage and make the case for why that difference matters?
questions.intent: Set up the sharpest ideological fault line in the segment — Edmund's inward, spiritual reading versus Daniel's structural, materialist reading — using a specific shared passage as the battleground

questions.question: Daniel, I have to press you on Agnes. You said — and this is a strong claim — that when Agnes says 'I have loved you all my life,' she's not freely choosing, she's been groomed to believe that loving David is her own autonomous desire. But Oliver and Edmund both feel that scene as emotionally true, even earned. Are you saying Dickens is condemning something he thinks he's celebrating? And if so, does that make the novel brilliant or does it make it a mess?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's most provocative take on Agnes as a site of coercion rather than transcendence, and directly invite Oliver and Edmund — who both have emotional investment in the reunion — to push back hard

questions.question: Oliver, you said something that I think is the hardest thing to resolve today — that in the Gray's Inn passage, David is escaping into fantasy, but Dickens is generous enough to let the fantasy be real at the same time. Daniel thinks those roses just make the law offices *tolerable*, which is worse than if they changed nothing. Edmund thinks the feminine warmth in that passage genuinely transfigures consciousness. Can all three of you be right? Or does one of those readings have to lose?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or collision on the Gray's Inn passage — this is the closing question designed to make all three experts' positions visible simultaneously and let the audience feel the irresolvability

steering_notes: The central fault line is between Edmund's inward moral reading, Oliver's narratological reading, and Daniel's structural-materialist reading — and they all converge on the same two or three passages. Keep the conversation anchored to specific language and specific passages rather than letting it drift into abstraction. When experts make large claims, push them back to the text: 'Can you show me where?' The 'no alloy of self' line is the fulcrum — it means something completely different to all three experts and should be returned to more than once. Watch for Edmund and Daniel talking past each other because they're not actually disagreeing about the novel's quality, they're disagreeing about what the novel *is for*. Oliver is the best bridge between them — use him to translate. Don't let Daniel's structural readings feel like prosecutions; his strongest moments are when he makes the structural argument feel like grief rather than verdict.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund reads 'no alloy of self' as achieved virtue; Oliver reads it as the sound of self-deception; Daniel reads it as performed selflessness that functions as control — all three need to be in the room at the same time on this line

Daniel's claim that Agnes has been 'groomed' directly contradicts Oliver's pre-interview point that the Agnes resolution 'works because Dickens earned it' — this is a genuine disagreement about whether emotional authenticity and structural coercion can coexist in the same scene

Edmund's insistence that the schoolroom mice are David's ego 'projected outward' is a direct and pointed rejection of Daniel's reading of them as evidence of class discipline — they should be asked to address each other explicitly rather than talked around

Oliver's reading of Mrs. Micawber as performing self-invention complements Daniel's argument that everyone in the novel is trained to mistake domination for freedom — this is a rare point of convergence that could briefly unite them before they diverge again on Agnes

segment_name: Atmosphere and Accident: How Setting Shapes Fate

questions.question: Oliver, you've said we should read Dickens aloud or we'll miss half the meaning. So let's start there — can you give us the Steerforth name-carving passage and tell us what you actually hear in it? Because I suspect what you hear and what Daniel hears are very different things.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the passage and articulate his rhythmic-incantatory reading, which sets up an immediate contrast with Rosen's structural-power reading and Leigh's moral-psychological reading

questions.question: Daniel, you've described Steerforth's kindness to young David as patronage, pure and simple — not salvation, not friendship, just a more pleasant form of domination. Edmund, I suspect, thinks that's letting David off the hook too easily. So Daniel, make the case: what exactly is Steerforth extracting from David in that school corridor, and why does it matter?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's structural power reading of the Steerforth-David relationship and provoke Leigh's counter that the real problem is David's failure of moral imagination, not the system

questions.question: Edmund, let's go to Uriah's prison speech — the 'I freely forgive you' passage. Oliver thinks it's a comic grotesque that lands like tragedy. Daniel thinks Uriah is genuinely, sincerely colonised by the reformatory system and that's the horror. You think it's spiritual corruption masquerading as piety. Can all three of those things be true at once, or does one of you have to be wrong?
questions.intent: Force a three-way confrontation on the Uriah passage — the comic vs. systemic vs. moral-psychological readings — and see if the experts find synthesis or genuine disagreement

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that Dickens writes with genuine pity for his poorest characters, but that his pity is the system's best tool. That's a pretty damning thing to say about a novelist everyone loves. Do you actually think Dickens knew what he was doing there, or is that the novel being more radical than its author?
questions.intent: Push Rosen to commit to his most provocative claim about Dickens's unconscious complicity, which should draw Leigh into defending Dickens as moral psychologist and Trevelyan into defending his performative genius

questions.question: Edmund, we have to end on the shipwreck — 'Rosa, come to me. He is dead.' Four words. All three of you want to quote it, which tells me something. But you each seem to hear something completely different in it. Edmund, you say it's consequent — Steerforth earned this. Is there any grief in those four words, or is Dickens just settling moral accounts?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage to dramatise the three readings in collision — Trevelyan's operatic restraint, Rosen's class-entrapment, Leigh's moral reckoning — and create a genuinely emotional close to the segment

steering_notes: The productive tension here is a three-way split that keeps shifting shape: Trevelyan hears music and performance, Rosen sees economic territory and power, Leigh diagnoses moral blindness. None of these fully contradict each other, which means the interesting move is to push each expert to explain why their framing is *primary* rather than complementary. Watch especially for Leigh and Rosen — they agree Steerforth's kindness is dangerous but for opposite reasons (Leigh blames David's discernment, Rosen blames the structure of patronage itself). That's the segment's sharpest edge. Keep Trevelyan performing where possible — he's the one who can make the passages *live* for listeners who haven't read the novel. Let Rosen be uncomfortable and let Leigh be precise. Don't let the Uriah discussion collapse into 'he's just a hypocrite' — all three experts know he's more interesting than that, and the disagreement about *how* he's more interesting is worth real time.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh explicitly anticipates Rosen will read the school system as producing Steerforth — make sure Rosen gets to respond to that directly rather than letting Leigh's framing stand unopposed

Rosen's claim that 'atmosphere is economic, not psychological' is a direct challenge to both Trevelyan's performative reading and Leigh's moral-psychological one — surface this conflict explicitly, ideally mid-segment

All three experts want to quote 'Rosa, come to me. He is dead!' — use this as a lightning-rod moment to show how the same four words can carry completely different moral weight depending on your framework

Trevelyan's insistence that character channels through setting (not the reverse) is closer to Leigh than to Rosen — if they find common ground here, push Rosen to hold his position or concede something

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about Dickens pulling off this sleight-of-hand — making us laugh at the school, then suddenly we're in this moonlit Romantic register with Steerforth, and by the time we notice the shift we've already fallen for him. Can you read that moonlight passage — c8:p58, the 'No veiled future' bit — and walk us through what Dickens is actually doing with the prose there?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage aloud and articulate the tonal shift argument, which sets up immediate tension with Daniel's reading of the same passage as an indictment of David's blindness to privilege

questions.question: Daniel, you told me before we started that you think that moonlight passage is actually a trap — that Dickens might not even know how radical what he's written is. Oliver just read it as tragedy and beauty. You're saying it's something darker than that, right?
questions.intent: Force the central disagreement between Oliver's 'reader seduced alongside David' reading and Daniel's systemic critique — the word 'trap' should provoke

questions.question: Edmund, both Oliver and Daniel have been circling around what David sees and doesn't see in that moonlight scene. But you've argued that the real moral hinge of this whole section isn't Steerforth in moonlight at all — it's a much quieter moment. David hears that Mr. Mell is poor, and says nothing. How much weight are you putting on that silence?
questions.intent: Pivot to Edmund's David-as-complicit argument, which cuts across both Oliver's reader-seduction thesis and Daniel's class-structure thesis by locating the failure in individual conscience rather than system or prose technique

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund is putting this on David's conscience — he knew, he chose to look away, that's the moral failure. You'd say that's almost letting the system off the hook, wouldn't you? That 'Exchange or Barter' detail — a child literally as a unit of debt settlement — that's not about David's character, that's about what the school actually is.
questions.intent: Set up the sharpest disagreement in the segment: individual moral failure versus systemic design. The 'Exchange or Barter' passage name-check should get Daniel to quote it directly

questions.question: Oliver, last word to you — Edmund says David failed a test of conscience, Daniel says the institution was designed to produce exactly that failure. You've been arguing the whole time that Dickens is teaching the reader something, not just describing David. So whose education is actually being completed here — David's, or ours?
questions.intent: Close the segment by forcing Oliver to synthesize or sharpen his reader-as-mirror argument against the other two positions, ideally producing a three-way response

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that should be kept live throughout: Edmund reads moral tragedy in individual conscience, Daniel reads class structure and systemic design, Oliver reads formal and readerly seduction. The risk is that Edmund and Daniel get into a binary argument and Oliver becomes referee — push back on that. Oliver's thesis is the most counterintuitive and should be kept in play. The moonlight passage (c8:p58) is the central battleground — get it read aloud early, ideally by Oliver, and let the others respond to the reading itself rather than an abstract description. The 'Exchange or Barter' detail is the best comic-to-grim pivot point if the conversation gets too abstract. If Daniel goes full structural-critique, ask him whether Dickens knew he was writing that — his pre-interview hint about authorial unconsciousness is genuinely provocative and the others will want to fight it.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's 'reader seduced alongside David' thesis directly contradicts Daniel's claim that the moonlight passage is a trap exposing David's blindness — they are reading the same three sentences as doing opposite things, and that should be made explicit on air

Edmund's focus on David's individual moral silence sits awkwardly between both positions: he agrees with Daniel that the silence matters but rejects the systemic explanation, and he agrees with Oliver that character is the key but denies the romantic framing — he should be pushed to say which reading he finds less wrong

Daniel's suggestion that Dickens 'doesn't know how radical this is' is the most incendiary claim in the pre-interviews and Edmund in particular is likely to push back hard — create space for that exchange after the moonlight passage is read

All three experts want to quote the phosphorus-box / ink-bottle sentence — let whoever gets there first read it, then ask the others whether they hear the same thing in it, since they each have a different interpretive frame for that theatrical image
